messages.subject: Appropriate use of multiple comparison adjustment following advanced.procD.lm()
messages.subject_clean: Appropriate use of multiple comparison adjustment following advanced.procD.lm()
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph community,

I'm comparing static allometric slopes of 38 species using advanced.procD.lm() and analyzing the pairwise p-values given by $P.slopes.dist. I know from a previous post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/geomorph-r-package/xGO9mCmxWu8/mPT8G_tsEgAJ> on this site that the test itself does not perform a multiple comparisons adjustment and that it is a user-based decision on what to do afterwards.

However, I have noticed that recent literature has not performed any adjustments on similarly large datasets. For example Esquerré et al (2017) <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/evo.13382> has 40 species of pythons and while they use an adjustment for their heterochrony test, they don't use an adjustment on their advanced.procD.lm() pairwise analysis of slopes. In their Methods, they state that the "Statistical significance [of the pairwise slopes test] was evaluated with a residual randomization permutation procedure with 10,000 iterations."

Is the permutation procedure alone sufficient? Looking at Adams and Collyer (2009) <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1558-5646.2009.00649.x#ss10> on comparing phenotypic trajectories (with my imperfect stats knowledge), I found this statement about the permutation procedure: "By performing many iterations, an empirical null distribution of a test statistic for the SSCP (sum of squares and cross-products) is created, and the significance of the observed statistic is inferred from its percentile in the null distribution."

Does this mean that no multiple comparison adjustment is needed because essentially the statistics (the p-values) come from one test?

Many thanks in advance for any advice or clarifications.

Best,
Ariel
Ariel E Marcy | PhD Candidate in Evolutionary Biology at The University of Queensland

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Appropriate use of multiple comparison adjustment following advanced.procD.lm()
messages.body_plain:
Ariel,

I would not over-interpret that quote as advocacy to disregard pairwise adjustments of alpha.  P-values for statistics are almost always estimated.  In parametric statistics, a theoretical probability distribution - like an F-, or t-distribution - might be used.  In geomorph, we generally use RRPP to generate empirical distributions.  The percentile of a statistic in the distribution is the estimate of the P-value (use fewer permutations and this estimate might be biased, if the true value is far lower than the number of permutations will allow to be estimated accurately).

You might be thinking of posthoc tests that adjust P-values.  This is one approach; the other is to adjust alpha.  Either way, one is attempting to ascertain the “significance” based on the established criterion.  In geomorph, we do not adjust the P-values but the user is free to adjust their pairwise alpha levels.  Inferring significance from the percentile of a statistic in its sampling (null) distribution (P-value), as stated, indicates nothing about what the alpha level should be.  That is the user’s choice.  A P-value of 0.03 might be “significant” for the user who does not adjust alpha levels but not significant for the user that does.  Nevertheless, 0.03 means that 3% of the time, the statistic was equalled or exceeded in random permutations.  Knowing this, one can infer the significance based on their own interpretation of whether 3% is low or high.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Colleagues,

I’m pleased to announce that geomorph 3.1.1 is now available on CRAN. As always, all changes are noted in the NEWS file and in the appropriate help pages. To install geomorph 3.1.1 from within R, simply type:

install.packages(‘geomorph’)

We wish to emphasize that this was a rather substantial update; thus, users are highly encouraged to consult all help files for additional information. Though some functions have been deprecated, all analyses previously available in geomorph are still available (though some more advanced options are now accessed in slightly modified form).  Also, to ease users through this transition, we have developed a vignette that describes the differences in the current version, and how to implement various analyses using the newer notation. The vignette is distributed with the installation of geomorph, and may be accessed by typing:

browseVignettes(package="geomorph")

In particular, users will notice a change in usage of the ‘procD’ family of functions for assessing linear models. Beginning with geomorph 3.1.1, only ‘procD.lm’ and ‘procD.pgls’ remain, and these have greatly enhanced functionality. For instance, one may now utilize type I, type II, or type III sums of squares, may specify the error term against which various factors are evaluated (to incorporate random effects in simple mixed model designs), and may incorporate object-covariance matrices describing non-independence.  Additionally, pairwise comparisons of means, of slopes, and of within-group variation may be accomplished using the ‘pairwise’ function based off of fitted models from ‘procD.lm’ or ‘procD.pgls’. The functions: procD.allometry, advanced.procD.lm, and nested.update, have all been deprecated, as their analyses are now accomplished (and enhanced) via these other functions. These enhancements were made possible by use of the RRPP package (Collyer and Adams, 2018: Methods Ecol. Evol) which is now more tightly interconnected with geomorph.

Finally, for graphical visualization of shapes, we encourage users to explore the new picknplot.shapes function, which allows one to select locations from just about any kind of plot obtained in geomorph, and generate estimates of shapes that correspond to those locations (much like in the TPS series). Also, the new plotAllometry function provides several graphical plots commonly used in allometric studies. We hope these new graphical options provide additional flexibility and usability of geomorph.

Best to all,

Dean, Mike, and Antigoni (the geomorph team)

Hi all,

I am using examples from the vignetts of the RRPP package to make sense of different types of sum of square. I managed to understand type I and II SS but have some confusions regarding type III SS, which is illustrated through the code below:

library(RRPP)
data("PupfishHeads")
PupfishHeads$logHeadSize <- log(PupfishHeads$headSize)

fit3 <- lm.rrpp(logHeadSize ~ sex + locality/year,
SS.type = "III", data = PupfishHeads, print.progress = FALSE)

anova(fit3, effect.type = "F")
#               Df      SS      MS     Rsq       F      Z Pr(>F)
#locality        1  0.0573 0.05733 0.00419  1.3562 0.7153  0.240
#sex             1  0.5554 0.55537 0.04064 13.1376 1.7486  0.001 **
#locality:year   6  1.6379 0.27298 0.11984  6.4574 3.1024  0.001 **
#Residuals     259 10.9489 0.04227 0.80111
#Total         267 13.6670

Since type III sum of square tests for the presence of a main effect after the other main effect and interaction, I think the following lines of code should replicate results from the above ANOVA regarding the effect of locality:

anova(lm.rrpp(logHeadSize ~ sex + locality:year, SS.type = "I", data = PupfishHeads, print.progress = FALSE),
      lm.rrpp(logHeadSize ~ sex + locality:year + locality, SS.type = "I", data = PupfishHeads, print.progress = FALSE))

However, thre resultant SS for locality is 1e-32, in contrast to the main effect of 0.0573 from ANOVA results:
                                             ResDf Df    RSS    SS MS     Rsq F Z     P Pr(>F)

Total                                          267    13.667

But I was able to replicate SS for the effect of sex through the following lines of code (the 0.55537 below is the same as the effect of sex from ANOVA results):

      lm.rrpp(logHeadSize ~ locality + locality:year + sex, SS.type = "I", data = PupfishHeads, print.progress = FALSE))

logHeadSize ~ locality + locality:year (Null)   260  1 11.504                 0.15825
logHeadSize ~ locality + locality:year + sex    259  1 10.949 0.55537 0.55537 0.19889 13.138 1.827
Total                                           267    13.667
                                                  P Pr(>F)
logHeadSize ~ locality + locality:year (Null)
logHeadSize ~ locality + locality:year + sex  0.001

I was also able to replicate the SS for the effect of locality:year through the following lines of code (the 1.6379 below is the same as the effect of locality:year from ANOVA results):

logHeadSize ~ sex + locality (Null)            265  1 12.587                0.079045
logHeadSize ~ sex + locality + locality:year   259  6 10.949 1.6379 0.27298 0.198885 6.4574 3.23
Total                                          267    13.667
                                                 P Pr(>F)
logHeadSize ~ sex + locality (Null)
logHeadSize ~ sex + locality + locality:year 0.001

I am therefore puzzled as to why thing go wrong only for the effect of locality, in the case of type III SS.

Thank you.

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Type III sum of square in RRPP package
messages.body_plain:
You happened to choose an example where the design matrix of one model (sex + locality:year + locality) is not full rank.  There is a case where one locality was sampled only in one year.  Therefore, the anovas of paired models - a bit more primitive in function than the multi-effect anova - is revealing in one case that the models compared have the same rank (df).  The multi-effect anova can adjust for effect rank, the paired model anova cannot.

I’ll have to think about whether to update the example or put a warning in the function, if this is confusing.  (The alternative is to throw an error, but then nested designs would be limited for analysis.)

The simplest explanation is that because of the design - one location sampled in one year, others sampled multiple times - the effects do not follow a null model - full model comparison in the traditional, most logical sense.  I can see that it looks misleading, as if the anova function is mixing up the models it is comparing, but I assure you this isn’t the case.  In the multi-effects ANOVA, QR decomposition is performed on the design matrices compared for each effect and makes sure they are appropriately ranked.  You will notice that the interaction had 6 df in your analysis, but here are the number of levels encountered by that term:

> nlevels(factor(paste(PupfishHeads$locality, PupfishHeads$year)))
[1] 8

So, although the ANOVA table shows the adjustment, the anova(model1, model2) approach just assumes you are comparing two appropriate models, and adding locality to a design that already had locality:year does not change the fitted values, as it becomes redundant.

I hope that makes sense, even if it is not comforting for this particular example.

Mike

On Tuesday, April 2, 2019 at 11:32:45 PM UTC+10, Michael Collyer wrote:

> Ariel,
>
> I would not over-interpret that quote as advocacy to disregard pairwise adjustments of alpha.  P-values for statistics are almost always estimated.  In parametric statistics, a theoretical probability distribution - like an F-, or t-distribution - might be used.  In geomorph, we generally use RRPP to generate empirical distributions.  The percentile of a statistic in the distribution is the estimate of the P-value (use fewer permutations and this estimate might be biased, if the true value is far lower than the number of permutations will allow to be estimated accurately).
>
> You might be thinking of posthoc tests that adjust P-values.  This is one approach; the other is to adjust alpha.  Either way, one is attempting to ascertain the “significance” based on the established criterion.  In geomorph, we do not adjust the P-values but the user is free to adjust their pairwise alpha levels.  Inferring significance from the percentile of a statistic in its sampling (null) distribution (P-value), as stated, indicates nothing about what the alpha level should be.  That is the user’s choice.  A P-value of 0.03 might be “significant” for the user who does not adjust alpha levels but not significant for the user that does.  Nevertheless, 0.03 means that 3% of the time, the statistic was equalled or exceeded in random permutations.  Knowing this, one can infer the significance based on their own interpretation of whether 3% is low or high.
>
> Cheers!

> Mike

messages.body_plain:
Grant,

I’m not sure what the functions in the HH package do (appears they are companion functions for a statistics text) but it appears you misinterpreted some of the output from a compare.pls object when using those functions.  It appears you used the $sample.z output as points in your plot and the $sample.r.sd <http://sample.r.sd> as error bars.  The SD values are not for the z-scores; they are for the r-pls values of the PLS analysis.  If you plot each sample's r-pls with these SD values as error bars, the analyses would not appear so conservative.

The z-scores are calculated from r-pls and the SD of r-pls as z =  (r.pls - mean)/SD, where mean is the mean of r-pls across the PLS permutations.  This is a summary statistic, not an estimate with a standard error.  There is no reason to plot z-scores and error bars.  Judging by your sample z-scores, which tend to be small, it is no surprise that the pairwise z-scores are also small.  If you do not have much integration in your samples, as a start, then it is unlikely, if not impossible, that you have large differences in integration between samples.  I think you were mislead by plotting standard deviations as error bars for the wrong statistics.

Hope that helps!
Mike

Natasa,

There are several steps to perform here, some particular to 3D meshes.

First, you need to generate predicted shapes along your CV axis. This may be done using the ‘shape.predictor’ function. The help file contains an example for shapes along PC axes, and the logic and implementation is the same.

Next, one obtains the mean specimen of the data using ‘mshape’. Then, for 2D data, the function plotRefToTarget will allow for TPS deformation grids between the mean and the predicted shapes you generated along the CV axis.  This will work for 3D also, but will generate TPS grids in the XY and XZ planes.

To generate warped meshes, one uses the aptly named ‘warpRefMesh’.  This will warp the mesh a specimen ‘back’ to the mean shape to generate a mesh for the mean shape (which obviously does not have one as it is not an actual specimen). Note this tends to perform better if you select a specimen that is already close to the mean shape in tangent space (see ‘findMeanSpec’).

Then, this may be warped into the predicted shapes along the CV axis using plotRefToTarget.

All of these analytical pipelines are described in the various help files of the functions listed above. I suggest you take a careful look at them.

messages.body_plain:
Peter,

First, I believe that performing GPA on all individuals before finding means is the better option, but it is an idea that could be debated.  If you do GPA by species, obtain the means, then do GPA again on species means, you have decided that each species’ “weight” in the GPA should be the same whether it comprises 1 or many individuals.  If it were me, I would not want species represented by a single specimen to have excessive influence on the mean shape and alignment in GPA.

Second, I don’t understand why coords.subset does not work when there is only one specimen.  I tried to simulate this an example and it appears to work

> data("pupfish")
> group <- factor(c(rep(1,50), 2, 3,3,3)) # the 51st specimen is the only member of group 2
> gp.coods <- coords.subset(pupfish$coords, group = group)
> means<- lapply(gp.coods, mshape)
> sum(means[[2]] -  pupfish$coords[,,51])
[1] 0 # the mean of group 2 and specimen 51 are the same

Third, in the method you used, when you reduced your factor you did not re-factor.  This is a common problem when removing values, as the factor levels still exist.  For example:

> levels(group)
[1] "1" "2" "3"
> group2 <- group[-51]
> levels(group2)
[1] "1" "2" "3"
> group2 <- factor(group2)
> levels(group2)
[1] "1" “3"

You will notice that just by removing specimen 51, factor level “2” did not disappear unless I specifically redescribed the reduced variable as a new factor.  If you ask R to subset data or find means by factor levels and for one level, there are no data, it will return NaN values.  This is not a geomorph trait; it is an R trait.

Hope this helps!
Mike

plot(mult_reg, method = "CAC")

Given that RSC1 represents the principal compoenent of the residuals of shape coordinates after size is regressed out, I would assume that this means that all differences between my different species (different colors) is explained by size. messages.body_plain:
Sergio,

I can only comment on some of the points you raised, as I cannot see the plot you attached, but I think it is worth considering the following:

- geomorph implements CAC and RSC exactly as proposed by Mitteroecker et al 2004

- "Given that RSC1 represents the principal component of the residuals of shape coordinates after size is regressed out..." notice that this is not exactly accurate, as to calculate CAC one first mean-centers each group. In this sense, then, only the part of shape variation associated to size that is COMMON to all groups is captured by CAC, and RSC is "residual" only in respect to that part of shape variation.

- In your case, it seems like assuming a common allometry, as is done under the CAC, might not be optimal. This is evident in your test for homogeneity of slopes, where the significant interaction between of CS and group suggests different groups have different allometric trajectories. This would make me consider to what extent you actually want to be looking at CAC, which is calculated under a single slope. It might be more useful to look at Regression Scores and Predicted lines to see how shape covaries with size across groups, or perform a pairwise comparison of slopes.

Finally, just as a side comment, note that procD.allometry has been deprecated in the most recent version of geomorph, released last week. To see how you can implement the same kind of analyses using the new functions, please see the vignette that is now included in the new version.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

To add and reconfirm,

Yes, geomorph calculates the CAC and RSC exactly as proposed in Mitteroecker et al. 2004. It is their method implemented in R.

Nearly half of your variation is explained by group differences, and explains considerably more variation than does the common (or separate) allometry. Unfortunately, Mitteroecker et al. 2004 did not provide their anova tables to explain how such effects relate to the patterns observed across the two plots; obfuscating understanding of their approach and what is expected in these plots.

messages.body_plain:
Samantha,

The function has a check to make sure the specimen names from your shape data match the row names of your gene expression data (assuming the data are in matrix form).  You say it was running “smoothly” before but this was not the case for certain errors.  The function used to align shape data and other data if and only if both had names that matched.  But if they did not match - for example, A, B, C, … and 1, 2, 3, … - then the function actually worked, assuming that both sets were in the same order.  That is a dangerous assumption!

This tighter security in the function might be inconvenient but easily overcome.  You have multiple choices, using “gene” and “shape” as your data names, and assuming your data are in the same order:

1. Assuming an array for shape data,
dimnames(shape)[[3]] <- rownames(gene)

2. Assuming a matrix for shape data,
rownames(shape) <- rownames(gene)

3. The other way around
rownames(gene) <- rownames(shape)
rownames(gene) <- dimnames(shape)[[3]]

4. Avoid it altogether
rownames(gene) <- NULL
dimnames(shape)[[3]] <- NULL

If your data are in different order, having names to match is imperative and the work-arounds above would only induce errors.

Hope that helps!
Mike

Therefore, for any particular modularity hypothesis, I run the analysis for all turtles in my data set, then for each subsequent turtle clade. So for each hypothesis I have a covariation ratio (CR) coefficient and a P-value for all turtles, and each family. Then, I have used the morphol.disparity function in the data set with all the turtles to measure morphological disparity in the proposed modules across all turtle clades.

I ask if it is acceptable to regress CR coefficients against Procustes variances to explore relationships between modularity and disparity?

Attached is an example. On the x-axis are CR coefficients from one of the well supported supported modularity hypothesis in which all the measurements I took of the legs and shell are one module, and the measurements of the head is another module. This hypothesis is also depicted by colors in the turtle silhouette. On the Y-axis are Procustes variances (although since I have linear measurements aren't they euclidean variances?) of the whole turtle body. Therefore, the disparity values correspond to the overall disparity of each major turtle clade, meaning the n x variables matrix I input into the function contains limb, shell, and head measurements. There are six major turtle clades in this graph, emydids (sliders and box turtles), geoemydids (old world wood turtles), pleurodira (side-neck turtles), kinosternids (mud turtles, stink-pots, snappers), testudinids (tortoises), trionychids (soft-shell turtles).

If I want to know if the strength of covariation between modules among turtle clades is related to morphology disparity of that clade is this okay to do?

Thank you so much for any insight.

Muchos saludos,
            Taggert

P.S. in X-axis it says high values= more integrated. I now realize that that isn't necessarily the case.

messages.body_plain:
Taggert,

I see nothing fundamentally wrong with regressing CR vs. variance to test for the suggested relationship between modularity and disparity. Why you would predict a non-linear relationship, as your graph suggests, or a linear one for that respect is another issue, which you need to consider from first principles beforehand. A useful recent read on the whole subject is the article by Felice et al Evolution (doi: 10.1111/evo.13608)

As for using morphol.disparity on linear measurements, yes, this is fine, as in that case you will obtain the sum of diagonal elements of the (group) covariance matrix divided by (group) sample size. This is called the Procrustes variance because it was put forward as a measure of disparity in the context of GM, but it can be used with any kind of data.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

Charles, to augment on Deans comment, in addition to be a statistically and methodologically better choice, working in full shape space will also allow you to directly visualize (full, as Dean comments) shape changes related to size, which is not the case with PC1.

And as a practical note, notice that procD.allometry has been deprecated in the last version of geomorph, and substituted by more general procedures through procD.lm. The vignette now included in the package provides very thorough support for how to implement analyses previously carried out using other procD.family functions, see, e.g. the new plotAllometry function for visualizing allometric variation, in combination with picknplot or plotRefToTarget for obtaining deformation grids in allometric space.

Antigoni

A useful recent read on the whole subject is the article by Felice et al Evolution (doi: 10.1111/evo.13608)
>

>
> Hope this helps
>
> Antigoni
> On 22/04/2019 05:38, taggertbu...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hey everyone!
> >
> > I am analyzing modularity, integration, and disparity across turtles. I have linear measurements of limbs, shells, and heads, not landmark data. So for each hypothesis I have a covariation ratio (CR) coefficient and a P-value for all turtles, and each family. Using ~1 obtains group disparities for each group based on the overall mean. These are equivalent to Foote’s partial disparities. The second equation obtains group disparities relative to a model containing group means.

Please see the help file, as this is explained there, along with examples.

Hi All,
So I am trying to plot the regression residuals from two types of ProcD.lm calls using CRC and RegScore. My understanding was that unless your data has a group structure to it, which mine does not, these should result in similar outcomes.
On a simple shape~single variable call,  I get very similar results between the two methods.
However, when I build my full model (with interaction terms), I get huge differences between the two methods. CRC appears forced linear, while RegScore does not.
Does anyone have an explanation for this?

Here are the model and graphing calls.
anova.genes.reg.nas <- procD.lm(coords ~ methylation* wnt9b * axin2, data= gdf.sub.reg.nas)
meth.multi.n.sz.graph <- plot(anova.genes.reg.nas, type="regression", predictor = subset$Methylation.Level, reg.type = "RegScore")
meth.multi.n.sz.graph <- plot(anova.genes.reg.nas, type="regression", predictor = subset$Methylation.Level, reg.type = “CRC”)

anova.meth.reg.nas <- procD.lm(coords ~ methylation, data= gdf.sub.reg.nas)
anova.wnt9b.reg.nas <- procD.lm(coords ~ wnt9b, data= gdf.sub.reg.nas)
wnt9b.n.sz.graph <- plot(anova.wnt9b.reg.nas, type="regression", predictor = subset$logddct_wnt9b, reg.type = "CRC”)
wnt9b.n.sz.graph1 <- plot(anova.wnt9b.reg.nas, type="regression", predictor = subset$logddct_wnt9b, reg.type = "RegScore")
meth.n.sz.graph <- plot(anova.meth.reg.nas, type="regression", predictor = subset$Methylation.Level, reg.type = "CRC”)

Thanks!!
Rebecca

Rebecca Green
Postdoctoral Fellow
Benedikt Hallgrimsson Lab
University of Calgary

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rebecca,

The common allometric component (CAC) and Regression score (and for that matter, a two-block PLS plot between shape and size) are all the same when there is no group factor.  What you are seeing (on one hand) as different is the first principal component score for the residuals (RSC1), which will naturally change as more terms are added to the model.  By eliminating residual variation with added terms, the scores will collapse toward a single line.  However, the example you provided also is because of a bug that we fixed (updated version on Github).  Note that the x-axis indicates “index” rather than your predictor.  This is a plotting error.  (On the other hand, this is causing your confusion.)

Also please note, the CRC plot option will be removed from plot.procD.lm (already removed on Github) because of the confusion it causes and because it is not model-based at all, but one can still plot CAC with the plotAllometry function.  We will launch version 3.1.2 on CRAN fairly soon but until then, the Github version of geomorph already has bug fixes included.

Cheers!
Mike
